vignette:
Dr. Alistair Finch presents as a man meticulously assembled. His tweed jacket is immaculate, his speech is precise, and he carries the quiet authority of someone who has spent two decades listening to the secrets of others. It took him four sessions to begin telling his own.

The story begins in 1996. He was 26, a doctoral candidate attending his first major academic conference in a sprawling, anonymous hotel. He describes himself then as “insufferably ambitious,” eager to network, to impress. He met a senior academic, a luminary in their field whose work Alistair had admired for years. The man took an interest in him, offering mentorship over drinks at the hotel bar. Alistair felt seen, validated. The evening blurred with conversation and too much whiskey. He remembers the man’s hand on his back, guiding him toward the elevators, the cloying scent of stale alcohol and expensive cologne.

He doesn’t narrate the events in the hotel room with linear clarity. Instead, he speaks in fragments of sensory memory: the scratchy wool of the man’s suit jacket against his cheek, the disorienting pattern of the hotel wallpaper, the chilling sound of his own silence. The overwhelming feeling was not pain, but a profound and paralyzing powerlessness. He describes it as a “cognitive whiteout,” a moment where the person he thought he was—strong, articulate, in control—simply ceased to exist.

In the morning, he left before the man woke up. He showered for nearly an hour, scrubbing his skin until it was raw, but the feeling of being unclean lingered for years. He never told anyone. He rationalized that he had been drunk, that he had sent the wrong signals, that fighting back would have ruined the career he was just starting to build. He buried the memory under a mountain of work, finishing his dissertation in record time, securing a prestigious post-doctoral position, and eventually opening his own private practice.

For over two decades, this strategy worked. He built a fortress of competence around the hollowed-out space inside him. He met and married Sarah, a warm and patient woman who accepted his occasional emotional distance as a quirk of his academic nature. He learned to manage intimacy on his own terms, maintaining a polite and sterile distance that she, to his immense guilt, never questioned. He became an expert in the architecture of trauma, guiding his own patients through their darkest memories, all while refusing to look at his own. He felt like a fraud, a cartographer who could map the terrain of others’ pain but was hopelessly lost in his own.

The carefully constructed walls began to crumble about six months ago. A new patient, a young man, sat in the chair opposite him and described a recent assault. As the patient spoke, Alistair felt a cold dread creep up his spine. The smell of the hand sanitizer on his desk suddenly became overpowering, reminiscent of the sterile scent of the hotel room. The low hum of the air conditioner sounded like the elevator’s drone. He found himself unable to speak, his mind a blank slate of roaring static. He had to cut the session short, feigning a sudden migraine.

Since then, the past is no longer content to stay buried. He wakes up gasping for air, the weight of a phantom body pressing him into his mattress. During the day, he is perpetually on edge, startling violently if Sarah touches his shoulder from behind. He finds himself snapping at her over minor things, a misplaced set of keys or a question asked at the wrong time, then retreating into a long, ashamed silence. He goes through the motions in his practice, but the words of his patients now echo in the empty chambers of his own unspoken experience. He sits in his office, surrounded by the books that taught him everything about the human mind, and feels a terrifying certainty that he knows nothing at all.
